title: I: The Prison-Door
focus: the prison door and the rose

teacherSummary.text: A crowd of bearded men and hooded women waits before the heavy, iron-studded door of the Boston prison. The narrator notes that every new colony soon needs a cemetery and a prison. Beside the door grows a wild rose-bush, which he offers to the reader as a symbol of some sweet moral blossom in a dark tale.

Foreshadowing: The narrator says the founders of every utopia soon need a cemetery and a prison. Watch for the rose-bush: Nature's possible kindness to the condemned.

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “The founders of a new colony, whatever Utopia of human virtue and happiness they might originally project, have invariably recognized it…” slowly and put it in my own words: The narrator says that whatever ideal society the founders imagined, they soon set aside land for a graveyard and a prison. Next, craft. I notice the irony of setting "Utopia of human virtue and happiness" against "cemetery" and "prison" in one sentence. The strongest word is “Utopia”: it names the perfect society the Puritans hoped for, and the rest of the sentence undercuts it. Then, effect. Why does the narrator say every new colony first builds a cemetery and a prison? My answer: The narrator says every new colony first builds a cemetery and a prison because even a community built on virtue must deal with death and sin; this sets up the prison door Hester walks out of.
